title: Event-Driven Architecture
summary: A command tells one known service to do something; an event announces that something already happened and does not care who is listening. Inverting that direction means a producer no longer knows its consumers — which is the whole payoff, and the source of every cost.
analogy: The difference between phoning a colleague to ask them to do something and pinning a notice on the office board. The phone call reaches one person and you hear whether it worked. The notice reaches everyone who happens to read the board, and a new team can start acting on it without you knowing they exist — but you also never find out that nobody read it, and someone who walks past the board an hour late is working from stale information while insisting they are up to date.

explanation.beginner: Normally a service calls another one and waits: 'create this invoice' — a command, aimed at one service that you know exists, and you find out immediately whether it worked. An event is the opposite. The order service writes 'OrderPlaced' to a broker and moves on. It does not know that an email service, an analytics service and a search indexer are all reading that message, and it does not wait for them. Adding a fourth listener needs no change to the order service at all. The price is that the order is placed before anything else has caught up, so for a moment the rest of the system has not heard about it yet.
explanation.interview: The distinction is intent and coupling: a command names a recipient and expects an outcome; an event is a past-tense fact with no recipient, so the producer's dependency on consumers is inverted. Transport is pub/sub (fan-out: every subscriber gets a copy) versus a work queue (competing consumers: exactly one worker takes the job) — see message-queue for the delivery, ordering and retry mechanics. Payload is a choice: event notification keeps the event thin and consumers call back for detail, adding load and latency but keeping the schema small; event-carried state transfer ships the data so consumers never call back, at the cost of the schema becoming a contract with everyone. Event sourcing stores the sequence of changes as the source of truth and derives current state by replay. Ordering is guaranteed per partition, never globally. Failure modes: visible eventual consistency, no stack trace across systems, and no single place showing the whole flow.

nodes.label: Order service
nodes.note: Publishes OrderPlaced and returns. It has no compile-time or runtime knowledge of who consumes it, and no code changes when a consumer is added.

nodes.label: Broker topic (partitioned)
nodes.note: Durably holds the event and fans it out to every subscriber group. Ordering holds within a partition — events for one order key stay in order; across the whole topic they do not.

without: The order service calls email, analytics and the search indexer directly and waits for each
Checkout latency is the sum of all three, and any one of them being down fails the order
Adding a fourth downstream means editing, testing and redeploying the order service — the team that owns checkout becomes the bottleneck for everyone else's features
with: The order service publishes once and returns; downstream work happens after the response
A slow or dead consumer builds lag instead of failing the order
A new consumer subscribes to the existing topic with zero changes to the producer
why.conclusion: The producer stops depending on its consumers — which is the real payoff, paid for with eventual consistency the user can see and a flow no single log shows end to end.

nodes.label: Email worker
nodes.note: Its own consumer group, its own offset. Being down for an hour means an hour of lag, not an hour of failed checkouts — but also an hour of customers wondering where their confirmation is.

nodes.label: Analytics worker
nodes.note: Added months after the order service shipped, without a single line changing in it. This is the payoff, concretely.

nodes.label: Search indexer
nodes.note: Writes a read model. It is seconds behind, which is why a user who just placed an order can search and not find it — the classic visible eventual consistency.

without: Checkout calls email, analytics and the indexer synchronously: user-visible latency is the sum of all of them, and p99 is the worst of all of them
Any downstream being unavailable fails the order — a broken analytics service costs you revenue
Every new downstream consumer is a change to the producer, so one team's roadmap gates everyone else's
Retry logic for each downstream lives in the producer, where a stuck retry holds a request thread
with: The producer publishes once and returns; the user waits only for the order to be recorded
A dead consumer accumulates lag and catches up, instead of failing the user's request
New consumers attach to the existing stream with no producer change at all
Load spikes are absorbed by the broker rather than by every downstream at once
why.conclusion: You trade an immediate, traceable answer for decoupling and absorption — and you take on eventual consistency users can see, plus debugging that spans systems with no stack trace to follow.

whenToUse: One thing happening has several independent consequences, and you expect more over time
The consequences do not need to finish before the user gets a response
Producer and consumer teams deploy on different schedules and should not block each other
Traffic is spiky and downstream work can be absorbed and drained rather than dropped
You need an audit trail of what happened, not just what the state is now
whenNotToUse: The caller needs the result to continue — 'was the card charged?' is a command with an answer, and wrapping it in an event just means inventing a correlation id and a timeout to fake a reply
A simple two-service flow where a direct call is honest: you would be adding a broker, consumer groups, dead-letter handling and lag monitoring to decouple two things that are not coupled painfully
A user-facing read must reflect a write immediately — if the list has to show the new item on the next page load, deriving that list asynchronously guarantees complaints
Strict global ordering is required across all entities, not just per key: brokers give you ordering inside a partition, and one partition means no parallelism
The team has no distributed tracing and no consumer-lag alerting — without observability an event-driven system fails silently, and 'it just never arrived' becomes a weekly occurrence

pros: You get the outcome immediately and can act on the failure right there
One stack trace covers the whole flow; debugging is ordinary debugging
No intermediate state — the write is visible to the next read
cons: Latency is the sum of the chain, and availability is the product of it
The caller must know every callee, so adding a consequence means changing the caller
A slow downstream applies backpressure straight into user-facing request threads

pros: Every subscriber gets its own copy at its own pace
New consumers cost the producer nothing
A slow consumer's lag is isolated to that consumer
cons: The producer has no idea whether anyone acted on the event, or whether anyone is listening at all
Each consumer needs its own retry, dead-letter and lag monitoring
Removing a field from an event breaks consumers you may not know about

pros: Exactly one worker takes each job, so scaling out is adding workers
Natural load levelling and straightforward retry semantics
cons: Only one consumer gets the message, so it is the wrong tool when several parties care
Ordering across workers is lost unless you partition by key — see message-queue for the mechanics

tradeoffs.option: Event notification (thin event, consumer calls back)
pros: Tiny, stable payload — mostly an id and an event type, so schema churn is low
The consumer always reads current data, avoiding decisions based on a stale snapshot
cons: Every consumer calls back, so a fan-out of N events becomes N callbacks and the coupling you removed reappears as read load
Adds a round trip of latency per consumer, and the callback can fail independently of the event

pros: Consumers need no callback, so the producer's read path is not hit at all
Consumers keep working while the producer is down
The event is a self-contained record of what was true at that moment
cons: The payload becomes a public contract with every current and future consumer — changing it is a coordinated migration
Duplicated state across services drifts, and consumers act on a snapshot that may already be out of date
Larger messages mean more broker storage and bandwidth

tradeoffs.option: Event sourcing (the event log is the source of truth)
pros: Complete audit trail for free — you can answer how the state got here, not just what it is
New read models are built by replaying history rather than backfilling
Temporal queries: what did this look like last Tuesday?
cons: Schema evolution is permanent work — you must still be able to read events written years ago
Rebuild time grows with total event count, so long-lived aggregates need snapshots or replay takes hours
Current state requires a projection, so every simple query is now indirect
Deleting a person's data from an append-only log is genuinely hard

keyNumbers.label: Synchronous chain of 3 calls at 20 ms each
keyNumbers.value: ~60 ms of user-visible latency, versus ~20 ms if two are events

keyNumbers.label: Publish to a broker, same datacentre
keyNumbers.value: ~1–10 ms, depending on how many replicas must acknowledge

keyNumbers.label: End-to-end propagation to a healthy consumer
keyNumbers.value: tens of milliseconds — seconds to minutes once a consumer falls behind

keyNumbers.label: Ordering guarantee
keyNumbers.value: per partition only; global ordering means one partition, and one partition means one consumer

keyNumbers.label: Cost of adding a consumer
keyNumbers.value: zero producer changes — the concrete payoff of the inversion

keyNumbers.label: Event-sourcing replay
keyNumbers.value: proportional to total events; snapshots bound it to events-since-snapshot

quiz.question: What actually distinguishes an event from a command?
options: Events are asynchronous and commands are synchronous
Events go through a broker and commands go over HTTP
A command names one recipient and expects something to happen; an event states a past fact with no recipient, so the producer does not know or care who consumes it
Events carry more data than commands
quiz.explanation: Transport and timing are consequences, not the definition — you can send a command over a queue and it is still a command. The real difference is the direction of the dependency: 'ChargeCard' names payments and expects an outcome, while 'OrderPlaced' is a fact and the producer's list of consumers is empty by design. That inversion is what lets you add a consumer without touching the producer.

quiz.question: A user saves a profile change, gets a success message, and the profile list still shows the old value for several seconds. The write went to the profile service; the list is a read model built by a consumer of ProfileUpdated. What is happening and what is the usual fix?
options: The event was lost; add a dead-letter queue
Ordering broke; use a single partition for the whole topic

Visible eventual consistency — the read model lags the write. Usual fixes: read your own writes from the authoritative service or a session-pinned cache, or have the UI show the value it just submitted until the event lands
The consumer is not idempotent; add a deduplication key
quiz.explanation: Nothing is broken — the system is behaving exactly as designed, and that is the point. The asynchronous read model is by definition behind the write, so the gap is a product decision, not a bug to debug. Options are to serve that one user's read from the source of truth, keep the submitted value in the client until the projection catches up, or accept and communicate the delay. Adding a dead-letter queue or a single partition addresses problems that are not occurring here.

quiz.question: A team wants to move from thin events (id plus type, consumers call back for detail) to fat events carrying the full entity. What do they gain and what do they take on?
options: They gain stronger ordering guarantees and take on more broker storage
They gain exactly-once delivery and take on higher latency

They remove the callback load and latency on the producer and keep consumers working while it is down — but the payload becomes a versioned contract with every consumer, and consumers now act on a snapshot that can already be stale
They gain the ability to replay history and take on a longer rebuild time
quiz.explanation: The callback in event notification quietly rebuilds the coupling you removed: N events become N reads against the producer, each adding latency and a new failure path. Shipping the state removes that, at the price of a schema that is now a contract you cannot change unilaterally, plus consumers holding copies that drift. Replay and rebuild time belong to event sourcing, which is a separate decision about whether the log is the source of truth.
